motion: Is stance-independent moral realism better supported than moral anti-realism?

routes.speaker: Michael Huemer
routes.position: Stance-independent moral realism is better supported.

bridges.statement: The overall balance of available reasons favors stance-independent moral realism over its anti-realist alternatives.
Clear moral appearances provide prima facie justification for objective moral truths unless defeated.
Non-cognitivism, subjectivism, and error theory each conflict with important features of moral thought or language.
Disagreement can be explained by bias and factual error, while convergence and progress remain compatible with moral knowledge.

routes.speaker: Don Loeb
routes.position: Moral anti-realism remains at least as plausible.

bridges.statement: The evidence is mixed and does not establish that stance-independent realism is better supported than anti-realism.
Moral seemings lack automatic realist warrant because their reliability and best explanation remain disputed.
Moral language and practice can be heterogeneous or express attitudes without committing speakers to stance-independent facts.
Disagreement, cultural influence, and non-realist explanations of convergence weaken the case for a truth-tracking moral faculty.

sections.title: Moral practice, values, and reasons for action
Convergence, moral progress, and comparative assessment

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
quoteEligibleExactSpans: if abortion is wrong then God is probably mad at us
moral statements didn't Express propositions
moves.attributionBasis: Huemer's uninterrupted opening statement begins at event 90.
moves.proposition: Moral clauses embed intelligibly in conditionals and other proposition-requiring constructions, supporting cognitivism over non-cognitivism.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Huemer's principal semantic argument and the debate's Frege–Geach-style consideration.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
quoteEligibleExactSpans: regardless of our attitude
it would still be wrong to torture babies
does not depend on the attitudes of observers
moves.attributionBasis: Clear continuation of Huemer's opening statement.
moves.proposition: Some acts would remain wrong even under universal approval, so their wrongness does not depend on observers' attitudes.
moves.inventoryRationale: Directly supports stance-independence against subjectivism and relativism.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
quoteEligibleExactSpans: what's wrong with nihilism
it's extraordinarily implausible
it was obviously morally wrong
moves.attributionBasis: Clear continuation of Huemer's opening statement.
moves.proposition: Error theory is extremely implausible because it denies even apparently obvious wrongs such as gratuitous lethal abuse of a baby.
moves.inventoryRationale: States Huemer's central intuitive objection to global moral error.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
quoteEligibleExactSpans: all the beliefs that are reasonable candidates
moves.attributionBasis: Huemer explicitly develops his epistemological view in his opening.
moves.proposition: All reasonable candidates for justified belief ultimately rest on appearances or seemings, so ethical intuitions are not epistemically anomalous.
moves.inventoryRationale: Supplies the general phenomenal-conservatist foundation for Huemer's moral epistemology.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
quoteEligibleExactSpans: can't check on perception without using perception
can't check on reason without using reason
intuitions that fit together and support each other
moves.attributionBasis: Clear Huemer opening turn.
moves.proposition: The inability to validate intuition without intuition is no worse than analogous circularity affecting perception, reason, and memory; mutual coherence can increase justification.
moves.inventoryRationale: Answers a standard challenge to intuition as a basic faculty.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
quoteEligibleExactSpans: existence of some controversies doesn't mean
moves.attributionBasis: Clear Huemer opening turn.
moves.proposition: Disagreement warrants reduced confidence on controversial questions but does not defeat noncontroversial moral judgments.
moves.inventoryRationale: Provides Huemer's qualified, non-dismissive answer to moral disagreement.

moves.speaker: Don Loeb
quoteEligibleExactSpans: evidence on both sides there
features of moral language that suggest
moves.attributionBasis: Uninterrupted Loeb opening statement.

responseComponents.component: Concedes assertive-looking linguistic evidence but argues that language use is empirical and that anti-realist self-understandings provide contrary evidence.

moves.proposition: Assertive features of moral language provide evidence for cognitivism, but contrary evidence leaves its semantics unsettled.
moves.inventoryRationale: Directly qualifies Huemer's semantic case rather than denying its evidence outright.

moves.speaker: Don Loeb
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I make moral assertions all the time
I do have values
moves.attributionBasis: Recognizable Loeb dialogue turn following Huemer's discussion of students.

responseComponents.component: Argues that making and reasoning with ordinary moral assertions need not reveal a realist semantic commitment.

moves.proposition: An anti-realist can make ordinary moral assertions and reason normatively while bracketing metaethics.
moves.inventoryRationale: Introduces the practice-based response to inferring realism from surface grammar.

moves.speaker: Don Loeb
quoteEligibleExactSpans: talk as though there are moral facts
a convenient shorthand
moves.attributionBasis: Continuous Loeb response.
moves.proposition: Talking as though moral facts exist is convenient shorthand for normative discussion and is compatible with anti-realism.
moves.inventoryRationale: Load-bearing defense of the practical coherence of anti-realist moral discourse.

moves.speaker: Don Loeb
quoteEligibleExactSpans: no determinate fact about what they're doing
moves.attributionBasis: Huemer asks for clarification and Loeb gives a clear answer; the question itself is excluded.

responseComponents.component: Offers heterogeneous use and semantic indeterminacy as alternatives to a single proposition-expressing analysis.

moves.proposition: Public moral language may lack one coherent analysis because speakers variously express attitudes, issue directives, or assert facts.
moves.inventoryRationale: Loeb's strongest semantic alternative to Huemer's uniform cognitivist inference.

moves.speaker: Don Loeb
quoteEligibleExactSpans: meta-ethics is at issue
we distract from the normative matters
moves.attributionBasis: Continuous Loeb explanation of post-error-theory practice.
moves.proposition: Making metaethical commitments salient during applied normative reasoning often distracts from the normative issue.
moves.inventoryRationale: Explains why ordinary and scholarly moral practice need not favor realism.

moves.speaker: Don Loeb
quoteEligibleExactSpans: a reflection of a moral feeling
look for a kind of consistency or coherence
available to me whether I'm a moral anti-realist or not
moves.attributionBasis: Continuous Loeb turn.
moves.proposition: Anti-realists can treat apparent intuitions as feelings or commitments and still test them against facts, coherence, and general principles.
moves.inventoryRationale: Shows how reflective-equilibrium reasoning remains available without stance-independent facts.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
quoteEligibleExactSpans: institution of morality is valuable
valuableness is one of those properties they think doesn't exist
moves.attributionBasis: Clear speaker change to Huemer in the alternating dialogue.

responseComponents.component: Challenges whether an error theorist can coherently describe morality as valuable.
Questions the normative basis for continuing moral practice under error theory.
Challenges the availability of evaluative assessment if evaluative properties do not exist.

moves.proposition: Error theorists cannot straightforwardly call moral practice valuable because value is among the properties their theory rejects.
moves.inventoryRationale: Major direct challenge to Loeb's account of anti-realist moral practice.

moves.speaker: Don Loeb
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there are other evaluative standpoints
serves our Collective goals
moves.attributionBasis: Clear Loeb response to Huemer's challenge.

responseComponents.component: Distinguishes stance-independent valuable properties from people valuing practices for shared goals and practical functions.

moves.proposition: An anti-realist may value morality's practical functions from shared or personal standpoints without positing objective moral value.
moves.inventoryRationale: Directly answers the alleged incoherence in anti-realist valuation.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
quoteEligibleExactSpans: you shouldn't say on your view
it really means something else
at least misleading to say
moves.attributionBasis: Recognizable Huemer turn after Loeb's clarification.

responseComponents.component: Argues that calling something valuable while meaning only that one favors it is at least misleading.

moves.proposition: Anti-realist moral talk trades on ordinary evaluative language while revising it into reports of attitudes, creating a misleading mismatch.
moves.inventoryRationale: Presses the semantic-pragmatic cost of Loeb's proposed reinterpretation.

moves.speaker: Don Loeb
quoteEligibleExactSpans: argument for moral experience
experience it as objective
moves.attributionBasis: Loeb explicitly identifies and reconstructs Huemer's argument in response to the moderator.

responseComponents.component: Reconstructs Huemer's case as requiring both objective moral experience and a defeasible entitlement to trust appearances.

moves.proposition: Huemer's argument from moral experience needs both an empirical premise that morality appears objective and an epistemic premise granting seemings prima facie authority.
moves.inventoryRationale: Clarifies the two independently contestable premises of the realist intuition argument.

moves.speaker: Don Loeb
quoteEligibleExactSpans: why we should take seemings as evidence for beings
that would be circular
things that seemed right to them
moves.attributionBasis: Continuous Loeb answer.

responseComponents.component: Denies that a seeming automatically warrants belief and warns that the entitlement cannot simply be presumed.
Argues that widespread application of the principle licenses implausible God and lottery beliefs.

moves.proposition: Treating seemings as self-authenticating risks circularity and licenses plainly dubious beliefs, so their evidential force requires further restriction.
moves.inventoryRationale: Central epistemological rebuttal to phenomenal conservatism.

moves.speaker: Don Loeb
quoteEligibleExactSpans: best explanation for things seeming
moves.attributionBasis: Continuous Loeb answer immediately before the moderator speaks.

responseComponents.component: Substitutes an explanationist condition: trust a seeming when truth best explains it, a condition Loeb says morality has not met.

moves.proposition: Seemings merit trust when their truth best explains the appearance; moral seemings have not yet satisfied that explanationist condition.
moves.inventoryRationale: States Loeb's positive alternative account of when appearances warrant belief.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I don't accept the explanationist requirement
fundamental epistemological principle
the most fundamental belief farming method
moves.attributionBasis: Moderator explicitly turns to Huemer, whose answer begins at event 1217.

responseComponents.component: Rejects explanationism as more fundamental than seemings because accepting explanationism itself must rest on what seems correct.

moves.proposition: The explanationist requirement cannot ground epistemology more fundamentally than appearances, since it too needs support from appearances.
moves.inventoryRationale: Huemer's direct foundational reply to Loeb's central epistemic requirement.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
quoteEligibleExactSpans: caused by your already being a Christian
those would be defeaters
moves.attributionBasis: Clear Huemer turn discussing religious seemings.
moves.proposition: A seeming can be defeated when cultural formation causally explains it and alternative cultures generate incompatible appearances.
moves.inventoryRationale: Important qualification showing Huemer's phenomenal conservatism admits causal and disagreement-based defeaters.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
quoteEligibleExactSpans: controversial moral issues
conflicting intuitions about a moral issue
you should not have compliment beliefs
moves.attributionBasis: Loeb explicitly compares Huemer's religious debunking to moral debunking; Huemer responds immediately.

responseComponents.component: Concedes that conflicting intuitions defeat confidence on controversial cases without conceding global moral skepticism.
Limits causal and disagreement-based defeat to cases where actual counterevidence is present.

moves.proposition: A conflicting moral intuition supplies a reason to doubt one's own intuition and reduce confidence.
moves.inventoryRationale: Preserves Huemer's key distinction between disputed peripheral cases and secure core judgments.

moves.speaker: Don Loeb
quoteEligibleExactSpans: cultural inputs and practicalities about of survival
moves.attributionBasis: Clear Loeb turn after the intuition discussion.

responseComponents.component: Suggests that even agreed moral judgments may arise from common culture and survival interests rather than apprehension of truth.
Challenges the proposed core-periphery distinction by offering one non-truth-tracking explanation for both agreement and disagreement.

moves.proposition: Shared moral judgments may be produced by culture and common survival interests rather than a faculty apprehending moral truth.
moves.inventoryRationale: Central causal-debunking alternative for explaining apparent moral knowledge.

moves.speaker: Don Loeb
quoteEligibleExactSpans: in cases where there's disagreement we should be skeptical
some better explanation
moves.attributionBasis: Continuous Loeb turn.

responseComponents.component: Concedes disagreement is not conclusive but argues that enough disagreement raises doubts about the truth-tracking explanation even for agreed cases.

moves.proposition: Moral disagreement does not conclusively refute realism, but its extent can make a non-intuitional explanation of apparent moral cognition more plausible.
moves.inventoryRationale: Captures Loeb's deliberately qualified disagreement argument.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
quoteEligibleExactSpans: a lot of disagreement in philosophy in general
not just in ethics
then I'd be more bothered
moves.attributionBasis: Clear Huemer reply after Loeb's disagreement argument.

responseComponents.component: Argues that ethical disagreement is less evidentially distinctive because unresolved disagreement pervades philosophy generally.

moves.proposition: Moral disagreement is not uniquely troubling because extensive disagreement occurs throughout philosophy.
moves.inventoryRationale: Huemer's main comparative reply to treating moral disagreement as special evidence against realism.

moves.speaker: Don Loeb
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we've undermined the hypothesis that there are auras
moves.attributionBasis: Clear Loeb analogy in the disagreement exchange.

responseComponents.component: Distinguishes domains with independent evidence for facts from domains where the disputed faculty supplies the principal evidence for both access and existence.

moves.proposition: Poor agreement can undermine only a claimed faculty when facts are independently established, but can also undermine the facts when that faculty supplies the best evidence for them.
moves.inventoryRationale: The playing-card/aura analogy is Loeb's most developed response to Huemer's cross-domain disagreement comparison.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
quoteEligibleExactSpans: people have a lot of biases
the progress of morality over the last 2000 years
moves.attributionBasis: Clear Huemer response to Loeb's request for an explanation of disagreement.

responseComponents.component: Offers self-interest, evolved emotion, and cultural bias as explanations of distorted intuitions.
Argues that decreasing racism and sexism show disagreement diminishing as bias is overcome.
Provides a truth-compatible causal account rather than treating poor agreement as evidence that the faculty is absent.

moves.proposition: Self-interest, evolved emotions, and cultural influences distort moral intuition, while apparent progress can result as some biases are overcome.
moves.inventoryRationale: Combines Huemer's debunking of error with his positive progress narrative.

moves.speaker: Don Loeb
quoteEligibleExactSpans: not nearly as confident in moral progress
authoritarianism is rearing its head
mostly people getting rid of biases
moves.attributionBasis: Immediate Loeb reply to Huemer's progress claim.

responseComponents.component: Questions both the stability of moral progress and the claim that apparent improvements principally reflect removal of bias.

moves.proposition: Recent authoritarian and racist reversals make progress less secure, and apparent improvement need not chiefly result from overcoming bias.
moves.inventoryRationale: Direct empirical qualification of Huemer's convergence narrative.

moves.speaker: Don Loeb
quoteEligibleExactSpans: agreement is a problem for moral anti-realists
moves.attributionBasis: Continuous Loeb response.

responseComponents.component: Concedes that bias, factual differences, and circumstances can defuse some disagreement.
Rejects the unsupported generalization that most disagreement is bias and that convergence is assured.

moves.proposition: Neither disagreement nor agreement is decisive: each creates explanatory pressure for one side, leaving the comparative evidence mixed.
moves.inventoryRationale: A major balanced concession that preserves Loeb's mixed-evidence stance.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
quoteEligibleExactSpans: before 1800 basically every society was was a dictatorship
about half the world is democratic
democracy is better than dictatorship
moves.attributionBasis: Clear Huemer reply in the progress discussion.

responseComponents.component: Answers recent reversals with the larger historical shift from near-universal dictatorship toward widespread democracy.

moves.proposition: Long-run political change from nearly universal dictatorship to widespread democracy is substantial moral progress plausibly explained by recognizing democracy's superiority.
moves.inventoryRationale: Concrete historical support for Huemer's convergence and progress claim.

moves.speaker: Don Loeb
quoteEligibleExactSpans: anti-realists can give perfectly
people don't like suffering
moves.attributionBasis: Immediate Loeb reply.

responseComponents.component: Explains democratization through reduced suffering and satisfaction of desires for control without invoking stance-independent moral facts.

moves.proposition: Anti-realism can explain democratization through shared aversion to suffering and desire for control, without positing recognition of moral facts.
moves.inventoryRationale: Supplies the requested non-realist explanation of apparent moral progress.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
quoteEligibleExactSpans: convergence on the non-moral facts
evidence of moral realism
self-evident moral truths
moves.attributionBasis: Huemer explicitly addresses the moderator's convergence objection.

responseComponents.component: Argues that moral convergence following correction of factual errors is itself expected if shared self-evident moral truths are operating.

moves.proposition: If agreement on non-moral facts produces moral convergence, that supports realism because factual error then explains the earlier moral disagreement.
moves.inventoryRationale: Huemer's clearest statement that convergence has positive evidential force for realism.

moves.speaker: Don Loeb
quoteEligibleExactSpans: anti-realism is the view that anything goes
utterly inconsistent with anti-realism
thinking that Hitler didn't do anything wrong is not the same thing
moves.attributionBasis: Clear Loeb turn responding to Huemer's repeated baby-torture example.

responseComponents.component: Distinguishes denial of objective wrongness from approval or permissibility, so stance-dependence does not imply acceptance of atrocities.
Rejects the portrayal of error theory as practical indifference or the claim that anything goes.

moves.proposition: Error theory denies objective wrongness and permissibility alike, but remains compatible with resolute opposition to torture and Nazism.
moves.inventoryRationale: Major clarification answering Huemer's most vivid objection to anti-realism.

moves.speaker: Don Loeb
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it seems to imply that it's okay
but it doesn't
moves.attributionBasis: Loeb directly continues his answer to Huemer's explanation of the example.

responseComponents.component: Suggests the intuitive force against error theory partly comes from conflating 'not objectively wrong' with 'okay,' a consequence Loeb rejects.

moves.proposition: The apparent obviousness of error theory's falsity may depend on mistakenly hearing 'not wrong' as 'okay,' rather than as denial of an objective property.
moves.inventoryRationale: Diagnoses a possible framework-dependent source of Huemer's intuitive reaction.

moves.speaker: Don Loeb
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I'm a pretty concessive anti-realist
it's up in the air
plenty to be said on both sides
moves.attributionBasis: Clear closing response by Loeb before the moderator's final question.
moves.proposition: The disagreement evidence leaves realism unresolved rather than refuted, and serious arguments remain on both sides.
moves.inventoryRationale: Important closing assessment preserving Loeb's repeated qualification that the evidence is mixed.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
quoteEligibleExactSpans: only your own appearances are sources of justification
justification is Agent relative
reason for doubting your intuition
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Huemer about peer disagreement; Huemer's substantive answer begins at event 2537.

responseComponents.component: Concedes that a comparably intelligent and informed person's conflicting intuition supplies a reason to doubt one's own.
Explains why disagreement can rationally divide agents without eliminating the initial justificatory force of each agent's own appearances.

moves.proposition: Justification begins agent-relatively with one's own appearances, but known disagreement from a comparable peer provides genuine counterevidence and should reduce confidence.
moves.inventoryRationale: Huemer's most precise closing concession about epistemic peers and intuition.

selectionRationale: The repaired inventory contains 35 chronologically ordered, independently assessable moves across seven source-required clusters. It includes each side in every section, stays within four moves per side per section, preserves Loeb's mixed-evidence qualifications, and distinguishes direct replies from constructive arguments. Two duplicate summaries were removed, every overlong span was narrowed, and five propositions were reduced to what a tight source span directly supports.
